<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line ltx_pruned_first">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Takuhiro Kaneko
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>NTT, Inc.
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Knowledge of the hidden interior structure of an object, including the presence and location of cavities, is essential for predictive simulation, robotic manipulation, and nondestructive inspection. However, such cavities leave no direct signature on the static visible surface, making collision-induced deformation one of the few cues used to infer their presence. Structure from Collision (SfC) addresses this problem by recovering the hidden interior structure of an object from multiview observations of a collision event. SfC is challenging for two reasons: hidden cavities are only indirectly observable through surface motion, and voids correspond to the absence of material, making direct optimization using standard density representations difficult. The density-based SfC baseline inherits both difficulties. Surface-matching gradients do not directly indicate the cavity location, while density gradients can be weak or uninformative inside or near void regions. Therefore, we reformulate SfC as hypothesis-space reasoning, representing hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses whose variables encode available structural assumptions rather than relying on implicit density updates. A global stage performs gradient-free optimization over this hypothesis space using forward-only material point method (MPM) simulation. A local stage then refines the selected hypothesis as a Lagrangian particle system through gradient-based optimization using differentiable MPM simulation. On the SfC benchmark, our method improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over the density-based SfC baseline. Interior-topology stress tests and robustness analyses characterize its scope and limitations.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
        The project page is available at <a href="https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/sfc-hypothesis/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/sfc-hypothesis/</a>.</span></span></span></p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span></p>
</div>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para"><img src="2611.07900v1/teaser.png" id="g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/258;" width="685" height="258" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
</div>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S0.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of Structure from Collision (SfC) via hypothesis-space reasoning.
(i) SfC infers the hidden interior structure from collision observations of objects with the same visible surface but different interiors.
(ii) A previous density-based SfC method <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> uses local density updates without an explicit hypothesis space, leading to ambiguous cavity localization.
(iii) Our method optimizes explicit structural hypotheses globally and refines the selected hypothesis as a Lagrangian particle system, yielding coherent interior reconstruction.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Vision-based 3D reconstruction is important for applications that require physical understanding, such as predictive simulation, robotic manipulation, and nondestructive inspection.
Recent methods have recovered detailed visible geometry and appearance from images or videos <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>.
However, visible geometry alone is insufficient to explain the physical behavior governed by internal mass distribution.
For example, as shown in Fig. <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(i), two objects with identical external surfaces but different hidden cavities are indistinguishable from static visual observations, yet can respond differently to the same collision.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Structure from Collision (SfC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> addresses this limitation by using collision-induced motion to infer the hidden interior structure from multiview observations.
Because post-collision surface motion reflects the internal mass distribution, cavities indistinguishable from the static appearance can be inferred from the deformation.
However, this inverse problem is difficult for two related reasons: hidden cavities are only indirectly observable, and void regions are difficult to optimize directly with standard density representations because they represent the absence of material.
As shown in Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Problem Definition ‣ 3 Problem Setup and Failure Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, the post-collision surface-motion discrepancy between a hidden-cavity object and its filled initialization can suggest an internal correction at a location different from the true cavity.
A previous density-based SfC method <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> inherits both difficulties. Without an explicit hypothesis space, surface-matching gradients may suggest corrections away from the true cavity, while density updates inside or near void regions can be weak or uninformative, leading to ambiguous cavity localization (Fig. <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(ii)).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To address these limitations, we reformulate SfC as hypothesis-space reasoning, replacing local density updates with explicit structural hypotheses evaluated against the observed collision response.
This representation directly encodes available structural assumptions in the hypothesis space rather than indirectly through a density field.
We instantiate this formulation in two complementary stages (Fig. <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(iii)).
The global stage performs gradient-free optimization over the hypothesis space using forward-only material point method (MPM) simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, while the local stage refines the selected hypothesis as a Lagrangian particle system through gradient-based optimization with differentiable MPM simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, recovering details beyond the initial hypothesis parameterization.
This two-stage design separates coarse structural reasoning from fine geometric refinement.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">On the SfC benchmark, the proposed method improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over the density-based SfC baseline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>.
Interior-topology stress tests and robustness analyses further characterize its scope and limitations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions are summarized as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We identify a structural failure mode of density-based SfC. Indirect surface cues and void regions make local density gradients unreliable for cavity localization.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We reformulate SfC as hypothesis-space reasoning, representing hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses rather than relying on implicit density updates.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a two-stage framework that combines gradient-free global hypothesis optimization with gradient-based Lagrangian particle refinement, separating hypothesis-level structural selection from particle-level geometric refinement.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate improved reconstruction and future prediction over the density-based SfC baseline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>, with interior-topology stress tests and robustness analyses clarifying the scope and limitations of the method.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3D reconstruction.</span>
Classical structure-from-motion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite> and multiview stereo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> recover surface geometry from images.
Neural 3D representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRF) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> and 3D Gaussian splatting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, further improve the reconstruction of visible geometry and appearance.
However, these methods primarily model visible properties and do not explicitly target the hidden interior structures that govern the physical response.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dynamic 3D reconstruction.</span>
3D reconstruction methods have been extended to dynamic and nonrigid scenes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>.
These methods typically learn deformation fields, canonical representations, and time-varying Gaussian primitives for temporally coherent reconstruction and dynamic view synthesis.
However, they primarily model visible motion and appearance, and do not explicitly target hidden interior structures revealed only indirectly through physical interaction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Physics-informed modeling and system identification.</span>
Recent studies have incorporated physical constraints or differentiable simulators to enforce plausible dynamics or estimate physical quantities from visual or multimodal observations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>.
However, these methods typically assume a fixed interior, even though internal mass distribution can strongly affect physical behavior.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Structure from Collision.</span>
SfC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> aims to recover internal cavity structures from collision-induced deformation.
The previous method, SfC-NeRF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>, optimizes volumetric densities in an Eulerian representation such that the simulated surface dynamics match the observed motion.
Although effective in some settings, this density-based formulation relies on local density updates without an explicit structural hypothesis space, which can result in ambiguous cavity localization.
In contrast, by representing hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses, we first optimize them globally and then refine the selected hypothesis as a Lagrangian particle system.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Problem Setup and Failure Analysis</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Problem Definition</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider the problem of inferring the hidden interior structure from visual observations of a collision event.
Given calibrated multiview videos <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\{\mathcal{I}_{i}(t_{j})\mid i=1,\ldots,M,\;j=1,\ldots,N\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathcal{I}_{i}(t_{j})\mid i=1,\ldots,M,\;j=1,\ldots,N\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of views and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of time steps, we obtain two observation streams: a time-varying visible surface <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}(t_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}(t_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> and image-space object masks <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}_{i}(t_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}_{i}(t_{j})</annotation></semantics></math>.
The surface <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}(t_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}(t_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> can be reconstructed from multiview observations using an off-the-shelf dynamic 3D reconstruction method <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>.
The masks <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}_{i}(t_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}_{i}(t_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> can be extracted using video matting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> or video object segmentation methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>.
These observations constrain the external geometry and motion of an object but do not directly reveal hidden cavities.
Thus, SfC aims to recover the hidden interior structure that shapes the collision response of an object rather than merely explaining the visible surface evolution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We represent the object as a particle-based continuum.
Let <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math> denote the ground-truth initial particle configuration and <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math> denote its estimate.
Given <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math> and physical material parameters <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta_{\mathrm{phys}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mi>phys</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta_{\mathrm{phys}}</annotation></semantics></math>, a physics simulator (e.g., MPM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>) predicts the evolving particle configurations <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_{j})</annotation></semantics></math>.
From these simulated configurations, we extract predicted surfaces <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{S}}(t_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{S}}(t_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> and render predicted masks <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i}(t_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i}(t_{j})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Thus, SfC can be formulated as an inverse problem: estimating an initial particle configuration <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math> that captures the hidden interior structure whose simulated surface and mask evolution match the observed collision dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Unless otherwise stated, we treat the physical material parameters <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta_{\mathrm{phys}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mi>phys</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta_{\mathrm{phys}}</annotation></semantics></math>, such as the Young’s modulus, Poisson’s ratio, and mass density, as given.
This controlled setting isolates the structural ambiguity from material-parameter ambiguity.
However, specifying these physical parameters does not specify the cavity; its location, shape, and topology remain unknown.
To assess the sensitivity of this assumption, we evaluate representative robustness settings in Section <a href="#S5.SS6" title="5.6 Robustness and Practical Considerations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.6</span></a>, with additional relaxed assumptions and physical-parameter error analyses in Appendices <a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 Robustness under Relaxed Assumptions ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a> and <a href="#A2.SS6" title="B.6 Robustness to Physical-Parameter Errors ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Under this formulation, a natural approach is to optimize the internal representation so that the predicted surfaces and masks match the observations.
However, density-based local optimization is structurally mismatched to hidden-cavity inference, as analyzed in the following subsection.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.07900v1/challenge.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:679/260;" width="679" height="260" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Misleading surface-motion cue for hidden-cavity localization.
An object with a left-side cavity (a) produces a leftward post-collision response (b), whereas the filled initialization used by a previous density-based SfC method (c) moves upward (d).
The resulting post-collision difference (e) suggests the removal of material from the right side, even though the true cavity lies on the left.
Thus, surface-matching cues alone do not reliably localize hidden cavities and can mislead local density-based optimization.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Why Density-Based Local Optimization Fails</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Problem Definition ‣ 3 Problem Setup and Failure Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates a representative failure mode.
A hidden cavity can induce a post-collision response whose surface-motion discrepancy points away from the true cavity location.
Thus, matching visible motion does not localize the area from which the material should be removed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This example reflects two coupled difficulties.
First, hidden cavities are only indirectly observable; surface or silhouette motion does not directly indicate which internal region is responsible.
Second, cavities are void regions (i.e., the absence of material), making it difficult to optimize them directly with density-based representations.
At the gradient level, local updates are driven by surface- or mask-level discrepancies. Near the visible surface, gradients tend to adjust the external motion or silhouettes, while inside or near void regions, little material exists to support informative density updates.
Consequently, local updates can reduce observation losses in directions misaligned with the true cavity, leading to ambiguous reconstructions and misleading minima.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">SfC-NeRF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> partially mitigates these issues by optimizing volumetric densities and applying volume annealing to escape the local minima.
Nevertheless, its optimization remains tied to local density updates starting from the filled initialization and lacks explicit space for structural alternatives.
Therefore, it can remain sensitive to initialization and may converge to cavity configurations that reduce local observation errors while remaining structurally inconsistent.
Together, these limitations motivate our formulation: we represent candidate cavities as explicit structural hypotheses and evaluate them before local particle-level refinement.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.07900v1/overview.png" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:679/302;" width="679" height="302" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of hypothesis-space reasoning for SfC.
(0) Dense particle initialization is reconstructed from multiview observations following GIC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>.
The initial rollout shows the dynamics before hypothesis optimization.
(I) Global hypothesis optimization consists of (1) instantiating cavity hypotheses and (2) scoring them with forward-only MPM simulation using a collision-adjacent loss.
(II) Lagrangian particle refinement: (3) the selected hypothesis is refined using differentiable MPM simulation with physical and geometric constraints.
This two-stage framework separates coarse structural reasoning from fine geometric refinement.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Method: Hypothesis-Space Reasoning</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Overview</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We instantiate SfC as hypothesis-space reasoning by representing hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses rather than relying on implicit density updates.
This shifts the optimization from local density updates to hypothesis-level evaluation in a low-dimensional space that can explicitly encode available structural assumptions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our method begins with a dense initialization, followed by two optimization stages (Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Why Density-Based Local Optimization Fails ‣ 3 Problem Setup and Failure Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
Following Gaussian-Informed Continuum (GIC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, we first reconstruct a fully dense particle representation from multiview observations (Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Why Density-Based Local Optimization Fails ‣ 3 Problem Setup and Failure Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(0)).
Unlike GIC, which uses this representation for physical-parameter identification under a fixed dense interior, we use it as an initialization for hidden-cavity reasoning.
Stage I performs gradient-free global hypothesis optimization by instantiating and evaluating cavity hypotheses with forward-only MPM simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> (Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Why Density-Based Local Optimization Fails ‣ 3 Problem Setup and Failure Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(1)–(2)).
Stage II performs gradient-based Lagrangian particle refinement of the selected hypothesis with differentiable MPM simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> (Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Why Density-Based Local Optimization Fails ‣ 3 Problem Setup and Failure Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(3)).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observation losses.</span>
For a set of time steps <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, we define</p>
<table id="S4.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{3D}}(\mathcal{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{3D}}(\mathcal{T})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{t_{j}\in\mathcal{T}}d_{\mathrm{CD}}\!\left(\mathcal{S}(t_{j}),\hat{\mathcal{S}}(t_{j})\right)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi></mrow></munder></mstyle><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>CD</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{t_{j}\in\mathcal{T}}d_{\mathrm{CD}}\!\left(\mathcal{S}(t_{j}),\hat{\mathcal{S}}(t_{j})\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S4.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{2D}}(\mathcal{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{2D}}(\mathcal{T})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{1}{M|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\sum_{t_{j}\in\mathcal{T}}\left\|\mathcal{A}_{i}(t_{j})-\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i}(t_{j})\right\|_{1}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi></mrow></munder></mstyle><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{1}{M|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\sum_{t_{j}\in\mathcal{T}}\left\|\mathcal{A}_{i}(t_{j})-\hat{\mathcal{A}}_{i}(t_{j})\right\|_{1}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{CD}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>CD</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{CD}}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the Chamfer distance (CD), and the predicted surfaces and masks are obtained by simulating and rendering the current particle configuration.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Structural Hypothesis Space</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We define a structural hypothesis space <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math> for candidate hidden cavities.
A structural hypothesis denotes a candidate cavity configuration evaluated and selected during optimization.
Starting from the dense particle initialization <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathrm{dense}}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>dense</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathrm{dense}}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math> (Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Why Density-Based Local Optimization Fails ‣ 3 Problem Setup and Failure Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(0)), a hypothesis <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h\in\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h\in\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math> specifies an internal void to instantiate (Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Why Density-Based Local Optimization Fails ‣ 3 Problem Setup and Failure Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(1)).
We parameterize <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> using compact structural variables, such as a cavity shape representation <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., an exterior-derived shape or a template index), center position <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝒄</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{c}</annotation></semantics></math>, size <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, and orientation <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝑹</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{R}</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=(\tau,\bm{c},s,\bm{R})\in\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝒄</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝑹</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=(\tau,\bm{c},s,\bm{R})\in\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Given <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>, we remove the specified material region from <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathrm{dense}}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>dense</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathrm{dense}}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math>, yielding the candidate particle configuration <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{h}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{h}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math>.
Unlike per-particle or per-voxel density representations, <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math> directly parameterizes structural hypothesis variables for the hidden-cavity inference.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            This instantiation can be extended with additional geometric variables or physical parameters, as evaluated in Section <a href="#S5.SS6" title="5.6 Robustness and Practical Considerations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.6</span></a>.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Structural assumptions define the hypothesis space by fixing or activating different variables.
We consider three settings with different amounts of structural information.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">(i) Known size.</em>
When the cavity size is specified, the search focuses on the cavity position.
The cavity shape is initialized by offsetting inward from the observed external surfaces rather than selected from predefined topology templates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">(ii) A set of candidate templates and known center.</em>
When the cavity center and a set of candidate templates are available, the center is fixed, while the template index and remaining configuration variables, such as orientation, are searched.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">(iii) Known template and center.</em>
When both the cavity template and center are specified, the hypothesis space is restricted to the remaining configuration variables, such as orientation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">These settings yield compact, low-dimensional hypothesis spaces for global exploration prior to particle-level refinement.
Their dataset-specific instantiations are described in Section <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a> and Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Model Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Global Hypothesis Optimization</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given the structural hypothesis space <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{H}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℋ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{H}</annotation></semantics></math>, the global stage selects a cavity hypothesis by evaluating candidate structures with forward-only simulation (Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Why Density-Based Local Optimization Fails ‣ 3 Problem Setup and Failure Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(2)).
Because each hypothesis removes material from the dense particle configuration, it induces a discrete structural change that is not well suited to local particle-gradient updates.
Therefore, we use gradient-free hypothesis-level optimization, with coarse-to-fine enumeration as the default for stability and reproducibility.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In other words, for each evaluated hypothesis <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>, we instantiate <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{h}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{h}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math> and perform forward-only MPM simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.
We define the base observation score using the 2D mask loss restricted to collision-adjacent frames.</p>
<table id="S4.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}(h)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{2D}}^{h}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{col}})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>global</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><mi>h</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mi>col</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}(h)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{2D}}^{h}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{col}}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{col}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mi>col</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{col}}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the frames immediately before and after the collision, and superscript <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> indicates masks rendered from the simulation initialized by hypothesis <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>.
Restricting the observation loss to 2D masks and collision-adjacent frames keeps the global stage focused on structural plausibility and avoids penalizing long-horizon discrepancies that an unrefined hypothesis cannot resolve.
For the position search, we augment this base score with a displacement regularizer normalized by the object extent to discourage disproportionately large cavity shifts, as detailed in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2.SSS3" title="A.2.3 Step (2). Global Hypothesis Optimization ‣ A.2 Model Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2.3</span></a>.
We select the lowest-loss hypothesis <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> and pass the corresponding particle configuration <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{h^{\ast}}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{h^{\ast}}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math> to the local-refinement stage.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Lagrangian Particle Refinement</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given the selected configuration <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{h^{\ast}}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msup><mi>h</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{h^{\ast}}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math>, the local stage refines particle positions to recover geometric details beyond the hypothesis parameterization (Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Why Density-Based Local Optimization Fails ‣ 3 Problem Setup and Failure Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>(3)).
Unlike the global stage, which evaluates discrete cavity hypotheses, this stage performs continuous particle-level optimization while preserving the selected cavity structure.
Following Lagrangian particle optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, we optimize the initial particle positions through differentiable MPM simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, which propagates observation-loss gradients through simulated dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The local stage uses the full observed sequence <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{all}}=\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{N}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mi>all</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{all}}=\{t_{1},\ldots,t_{N}\}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{local}}={}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>local</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{local}}={}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{3D}}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{all}})+\lambda_{\mathrm{2D}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{2D}}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{all}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mi>all</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mi>all</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{3D}}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{all}})+\lambda_{\mathrm{2D}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{2D}}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{all}})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S4.E4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{rep}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rep}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{vol}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vol}}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>rep</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>rep</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>vol</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>vol</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{rep}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rep}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{vol}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vol}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">This full-sequence objective complements the collision-adjacent mask loss in the global stage by refining the particle-level geometry and dynamics over the entire trajectory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To stabilize the refinement around the selected hypothesis, we use two geometry-aware regularization losses.
The repulsive loss is</p>
<table id="S4.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rep}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{rep}}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{rep}}}\left(\frac{\|\hat{p}_{i}(t_{1})-\hat{p}_{j}(t_{1})\|}{d_{\mathrm{grid}}}-1\right)^{2}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>rep</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mi>rep</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mi>rep</mi></msub></mrow></munder></mstyle><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>grid</mi></msub></mfrac></mstyle><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rep}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{rep}}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{rep}}}\left(\frac{\|\hat{p}_{i}(t_{1})-\hat{p}_{j}(t_{1})\|}{d_{\mathrm{grid}}}-1\right)^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}_{i}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}_{i}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the position of the <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>th particle in <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{rep}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mi>rep</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{rep}}</annotation></semantics></math> contains nearby particle pairs, and <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{grid}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>grid</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{grid}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the grid spacing.
This loss discourages particle collapse and excessive clustering.
The volume-preservation loss is</p>
<table id="S4.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vol}}=\left(\frac{\mathcal{V}(\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_{1}))+\epsilon}{\mathcal{V}(\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathrm{ref}}(t_{1}))+\epsilon}-1\right)^{2}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>vol</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>ref</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vol}}=\left(\frac{\mathcal{V}(\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_{1}))+\epsilon}{\mathcal{V}(\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathrm{ref}}(t_{1}))+\epsilon}-1\right)^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the estimated material volume of the particle configuration, <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathrm{ref}}(t_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>ref</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathrm{ref}}(t_{1})</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the reference configuration, and <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a small constant.
The reference can either be fixed to the selected hypothesis or updated during refinement.
We use the latter adaptive variant by default.
Together, these losses allow local adjustment while preserving the coarse structure selected in the global stage.
Loss-design ablations are provided in Section <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Implementation and Complexity</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implementation.</span>
We kept the hypothesis-grid resolution, MPM time step, refinement steps, and loss weights <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\mathrm{2D}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\mathrm{2D}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\mathrm{rep}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>rep</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\mathrm{rep}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{\mathrm{vol}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>vol</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{\mathrm{vol}}</annotation></semantics></math> fixed across experiments unless otherwise stated.
We used the physical parameters <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Theta_{\mathrm{phys}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mi>phys</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Theta_{\mathrm{phys}}</annotation></semantics></math> from the previous SfC setting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>, such that the evaluation focuses on structural inference rather than material-parameter estimation.
In relaxed settings, physical parameters can be included as additional variables, as evaluated in Section <a href="#S5.SS6" title="5.6 Robustness and Practical Considerations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.6</span></a>.
Additional implementation details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Model Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Complexity.</span>
The global and local stages have different computational profiles.
The global stage evaluates the cavity hypotheses with forward-only MPM simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> on collision-adjacent frames without backpropagation.
For an exhaustive grid with <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> samples per dimension in a <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional hypothesis space, the cost scales as <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(n^{d})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(n^{d})</annotation></semantics></math> forward simulations.
In our default coarse-to-fine setting, this stage used 250 forward simulations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The local stage is more expensive per iteration because it performs forward–backward differentiable MPM simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> over the full observed sequence.
We used 2,000 Lagrangian particle refinement iterations in the default setting.
In a representative timing measurement, the global search accounted for approximately 3% of the local-refinement runtime because each global evaluation is forward-only and uses fewer frames.
We provide detailed runtime analysis in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS8" title="B.8 Runtime Analysis ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.8</span></a> and optimizer ablations in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Global Optimizer and Refinement Ablation ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Datasets.</span>
We evaluated our method on the standard SfC benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> and the Topology dataset.
The SfC benchmark contains 40 sequences over five external shapes (<span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">sphere</span>, <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">cube</span>, <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">bicone</span>, <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">cylinder</span>, and <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">diamond</span>) with four cavity sizes and four cavity positions.
The Topology dataset is designed as an interior-topology stress test with 60 configurations grouped into <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">symmetric</span>, <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">asymmetric</span>, and <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">complex</span> subsets.
Detailed dataset construction and representative examples are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Dataset ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines.</span>
