<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>Ablation study of global optimizers and Lagrangian particle refinement on the SfC benchmark under cavity position variation.
<em id="A2.T7.12" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Global evals</em> denotes the number of forward-only MPM simulations used in the global stage.
<em id="A2.T7.13" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Fine stage</em> indicates whether grid refinement is applied after the initial global search.
<em id="A2.T7.14" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Local refine</em> indicates whether the selected hypothesis is refined with differentiable MPM simulation.
All global optimizers use the same objective and search ranges.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyzed the contributions of global hypothesis optimization and local refinement under cavity position variation, where cavity localization is most ambiguous.
This analysis extends the framework-stage ablation in Section <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a> and the optimizer-sensitivity evaluation in Section <a href="#S5.SS6" title="5.6 Robustness and Practical Considerations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.6</span></a> of the main paper.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We compared the default coarse-to-fine grid enumeration with random search and CMA-ES <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>.
For grid and random search, the 125-evaluation setting uses only the coarse stage, whereas the 250-evaluation setting uses 125 coarse evaluations followed by 125 fine evaluations around the best coarse candidate.
Random search replaces coarse grid enumeration with uniform sampling over the same search ranges.
CMA-ES uses the same evaluation budgets without a separate coarse/fine split.
All global optimizer configurations use the same objective and search ranges.
For each configuration, we evaluated the selected hypothesis with and without Lagrangian particle refinement.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ B.1 Global Optimizer and Refinement Ablation ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> shows three main trends:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(i) Limitations of local refinement.</span>
Local refinement alone improves over instantiation only, but remains limited by the initial cavity placement.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(ii) Effects of global hypothesis optimization.</span>
Adding global hypothesis optimization improves reconstruction before refinement, and combining global optimization with Lagrangian particle refinement gives the strongest results.
For the default grid optimizer, the coarse-to-fine search improves over the coarse-only search, showing that the fine search stage is useful in this hypothesis space.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(iii) Optimizer sensitivity.</span>
Alternative gradient-free optimizers achieve comparable performance under matched or comparable evaluation budgets.
CMA-ES reaches a strong solution with only 125 evaluations, but increasing its budget to 250 evaluations does not further improve performance in this low-dimensional hypothesis space.
The default coarse-to-fine grid enumeration achieves comparable final accuracy, indicating that it is a reasonable and reproducible choice for the current hypothesis space.
Overall, these results suggest that the performance gains primarily arise from hypothesis-level evaluation and subsequent Lagrangian particle refinement, rather than from the choice of global optimizer.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Additional Interior-Topology Results</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide supplementary results for the interior-topology stress tests in Section <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Interior-Topology Stress Tests ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a> of the main paper.
We first report F-score results corresponding to the main-paper CD results (Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2.SSS1" title="B.2.1 F-score Results for Interior-Topology Stress Tests ‣ B.2 Additional Interior-Topology Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2.1</span></a>), and then provide an additional ablation on the asymmetric subset to analyze how the global and local stages behave when the dominant ambiguity lies in cavity shape (Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2.SSS2" title="B.2.2 Ablation on the Asymmetric Topology Subset ‣ B.2 Additional Interior-Topology Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.1 </span>F-score Results for Interior-Topology Stress Tests</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ B.2.1 F-score Results for Interior-Topology Stress Tests ‣ B.2 Additional Interior-Topology Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> reports F-score results for the interior-topology stress tests corresponding to the CD results in Section <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Interior-Topology Stress Tests ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a>.
Overall, the F-score results show a trend consistent with the CD results in the main paper:
Under the known-size setting, our method improves over SfC-NeRF across all topology subsets.
When stronger structural assumptions are available, the F-score remains stable or improves across the topology subsets.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Compared with CD, the difference between the template-candidate setting and the known-template setting is smaller in F-score.
This is consistent with F-score being a thresholded metric that is less sensitive than CD to fine geometric deviations.
Although this thresholding compresses the gap between the two stronger-assumption settings, the overall trend remains consistent with the main-paper CD results.
Thus, the F-score results provide complementary support for the same overall trend.</p>
</div>

<section id="A2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.2 </span>Ablation on the Asymmetric Topology Subset</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further analyzed the asymmetric subset of the Topology dataset to complement the interior-topology stress tests in Section <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Interior-Topology Stress Tests ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a> of the main paper.
We chose this subset because its cavities break symmetry and introduce preferred orientations, creating a clear shape mismatch with the inner-surface initialization derived from the external geometry.
Unlike the cavity-position setting in the SfC benchmark, this setting primarily changes the cavity shape rather than its location.
This makes the experiment useful for examining how the global and local stages behave when the dominant ambiguity lies in cavity shape.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ B.2.2 Ablation on the Asymmetric Topology Subset ‣ B.2 Additional Interior-Topology Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> provides an ablation complementary to the position-variation analysis in the main paper.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stage-wise ablation.</span>
Local refinement alone gives a large improvement over instantiation only, suggesting that particle-level adjustment is particularly useful when the initial hypothesis has a shape mismatch.
Global optimization alone also improves over instantiation only, although its effect is smaller than local refinement in this shape-mismatch setting.
The full pipeline achieves the best CD, indicating that global hypothesis optimization and Lagrangian particle refinement remain complementary, while their relative contributions depend on the dominant source of ambiguity.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.SSS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Geometry-aware losses.</span>
The fixed volume-preservation loss slightly degrades CD, likely because asymmetric cavities require larger shape adjustment and a fixed reference volume can be overly restrictive.
The adaptive volume-preservation loss improves reconstruction by updating the reference configuration during refinement.
F-score changes only marginally across configurations, suggesting that it is less sensitive than CD to the geometric differences observed in this setting.</p>
</div>

<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Effect of Initialization Source</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">SfC-NeRF uses Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, a voxel-based NeRF representation, for initialization, whereas our default implementation uses 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>.
To isolate the influence of the initialization source, we additionally initialized our optimization from DVGO reconstructions by thresholding the learned alpha grid and sampling particle positions from occupied voxels.
For this DVGO-based initialization variant, the deformation network used for surface extraction is unavailable, so we disabled the 3D surface loss.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ B.3 Effect of Initialization Source ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> compares different combinations of initialization sources and optimization frameworks.
Even when initialized from the same DVGO reconstruction used by SfC-NeRF, our optimization framework improves over SfC-NeRF.
Using the default 3DGS initialization further improves reconstruction accuracy.
These results indicate that the proposed optimization framework contributes substantially to the performance gain, while the initialization source provides additional improvement.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 12: </span>Future prediction accuracy on the Topology dataset under symmetric, asymmetric, and complex subsets.
All methods are optimized using 14 observed frames and evaluated at <math id="A2.T12.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+7</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.T12.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+14" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+14</annotation></semantics></math> future frames.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report additional quantitative results for future prediction on the SfC and Topology datasets.
These results complement the analysis in Section <a href="#S5.SS5" title="5.5 Future Prediction ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.5</span></a> of the main paper.
All methods are optimized using <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=14" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=14</annotation></semantics></math> observed frames and evaluated at <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+7</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+14" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+14</annotation></semantics></math> future frames.
GIC and our variants use the GIC-based rendering pipeline described in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2.SSS5" title="A.2.5 Re-optimizing Gaussian Attributes ‣ A.2 Model Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2.5</span></a>, whereas SfC-NeRF uses its original PAC-NeRF-based rendering pipeline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">SfC benchmark.</span>
On the SfC benchmark, Table <a href="#A2.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ B.4 Additional Future Prediction Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> reports results under cavity size and position variations.
Our full model achieves the best performance for all settings and prediction horizons.
The gains are substantial under both variations, demonstrating the strong end-to-end future-prediction performance of our full framework.
For example, at <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+14" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+14</annotation></semantics></math> frames under position variation, our method improves PSNR by more than 5 dB over SfC-NeRF.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Topology dataset.</span>
Table <a href="#A2.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ B.4 Additional Future Prediction Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> reports results on the Topology dataset under symmetric, asymmetric, and complex subsets.
Our full model outperforms all baselines for every subset and prediction horizon.
The gap between the global-only variant and the full model indicates that Lagrangian particle refinement is important for future prediction, especially for complex interior structures.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Together, these results show that global hypothesis optimization and Lagrangian particle refinement provide complementary benefits for future prediction under diverse geometry and topology conditions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.5 </span>Robustness under Relaxed Assumptions</h3>

<div id="A2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated robustness by relaxing controlled assumptions used in the main experiments.
Specifically, we considered two settings: <span id="A2.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unknown cavity size</span> and <span id="A2.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unknown physical parameters</span>.
For each setting, global hypothesis optimization is extended to include the corresponding variables.
The search ranges and grid resolutions are summarized in Table <a href="#A1.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ A.2.3 Step (2). Global Hypothesis Optimization ‣ A.2 Model Details ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.
These relaxed settings test whether the framework remains effective when part of the structural or physical information is not provided.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS5.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.5.1 </span>Unknown Cavity Size</h4>

<div id="A2.SS5.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS5.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated the unknown-size setting on the SfC benchmark under both cavity size and position variations.
The cavity size is estimated jointly with cavity position by extending the global hypothesis space to include size as an additional variable.
For SfC-NeRF, the mass loss term is removed to avoid relying on the known-size assumption.
Table <a href="#A2.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ B.5.1 Unknown Cavity Size ‣ B.5 Robustness under Relaxed Assumptions ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> summarizes the results.
Compared with the known-size setting, the unknown-size setting degrades reconstruction accuracy, but our method remains substantially better than SfC-NeRF under both assumption settings.
These results indicate that the proposed framework can incorporate cavity size into hypothesis-level optimization without requiring it to be fixed in advance.</p>
</div>

<em id="A2.T13.11" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Known</em> indicates that the cavity size is provided, while <em id="A2.T13.12" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Unknown</em> estimates the cavity size jointly with cavity position.

<section id="A2.SS5.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.5.2 </span>Unknown Physical Parameters</h4>

<div id="A2.SS5.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS5.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated robustness when the physical parameters, namely Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio, are unknown.
The global hypothesis space is extended to jointly search cavity position and physical parameters, both of which are further optimized during local refinement.
For SfC-NeRF, the physical parameters are optimized together with the reconstruction variables, using the ground-truth values as initialization to provide a favorable condition.
Table <a href="#A2.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ B.5.2 Unknown Physical Parameters ‣ B.5 Robustness under Relaxed Assumptions ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> shows that our method exhibits only minor degradation compared with the known-parameter setting while outperforming SfC-NeRF under both assumption settings.
Table <a href="#A2.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ B.5.2 Unknown Physical Parameters ‣ B.5 Robustness under Relaxed Assumptions ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> further shows that our method achieves lower estimation errors for both Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 15: </span>Physical-parameter estimation errors in the unknown-parameter setting.
We report the mean absolute errors of Young’s modulus <math id="A2.T15.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log_{10}E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>10</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log_{10}E</annotation></semantics></math> and Poisson’s ratio <math id="A2.T15.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math> under the size- and position-variation settings of the SfC benchmark.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS5.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS5.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS5.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Summary.</span>
The proposed framework remains stable when cavity size or physical parameters are not provided.
These results support the robustness of hypothesis-space reasoning under relaxed structural and physical assumptions.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.6 </span>Robustness to Physical-Parameter Errors</h3>

<div id="A2.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further evaluated sensitivity to physical-parameter misspecification, extending the representative <math id="A2.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 10\%</annotation></semantics></math> error results reported in Table <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 5.6 Robustness and Practical Considerations ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> of the main paper.
Unlike the unknown-parameter setting in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 Robustness under Relaxed Assumptions ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a>, the physical parameters are provided to the method but are perturbed from the ground-truth values.
We evaluated larger perturbations of <math id="A2.SS6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 20\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 30\%</annotation></semantics></math> for Young’s modulus <math id="A2.SS6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> and Poisson’s ratio <math id="A2.SS6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math> on sphere objects under cavity size and position variations.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ B.6 Robustness to Physical-Parameter Errors ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> summarizes the results.
Errors in Young’s modulus lead to a gradual degradation as the perturbation magnitude increases, especially under cavity position variation.
This is consistent with stiffness directly affecting post-collision deformation, so an incorrect stiffness value can make cavity localization from motion cues more difficult.
In contrast, errors in Poisson’s ratio have little effect in this setting: even under <math id="A2.SS6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 30\%</annotation></semantics></math> perturbations, the results remain close to the clean setting for both size and position variations.
Overall, these results indicate that the framework is robust to moderate physical-parameter errors, while large stiffness errors can degrade reconstruction when cavity localization is ambiguous.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 17: </span>Robustness to Young’s modulus across geometry settings.
We report CD<math id="A2.T17.m55" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math> and F-score (F<math id="A2.T17.m56" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math>) under (a) external-shape, (b) cavity-size, and (c) cavity-position variations.
Avg. represents the average over the five Young’s modulus settings.
CD values are scaled by <math id="A2.T17.m57" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>

Avg. represents the average over the five Poisson’s ratio settings.

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;">(c) Cavity-position variation</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 19: </span>Robustness across material models and geometry settings.
We report CD<math id="A2.T19.m34" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math> and F-score (F<math id="A2.T19.m35" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math>) under (a) external-shape, (b) cavity-size, and (c) cavity-position variations.
Results for Newtonian, non-Newtonian, and plasticine are averaged over two parameter settings per material category.
Avg. is computed over all evaluated material settings.
CD values are scaled by <math id="A2.T19.m36" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While the main experiments use the material-fixed subset of the SfC benchmark, the SfC dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> also provides material variations under controlled geometry.
Here, we used these variations to evaluate whether reconstruction remains stable under changes in material properties and models.
This analysis differs from the unknown-parameter setting in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS5" title="B.5 Robustness under Relaxed Assumptions ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.5</span></a>: the physical parameters are provided for each sequence rather than estimated, while either the parameter values or the material model differs from the default elastic setting.
Thus, the goal is to evaluate robustness to material variations rather than physical-parameter estimation accuracy.
We organized the evaluation along two axes: material variation and geometry setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Material axis.</span>
We evaluated three types of material variation from the SfC dataset:
<span id="A2.SS7.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(i) Young’s modulus variation</span>, where <math id="A2.SS7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> is varied over
<math id="A2.SS7.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{2.5\times 10^{5},5.0\times 10^{5},1.0\times 10^{6},2.0\times 10^{6},4.0\times 10^{6}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>5</mn></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>5.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>5</mn></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>1.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>2.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>4.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{2.5\times 10^{5},5.0\times 10^{5},1.0\times 10^{6},2.0\times 10^{6},4.0\times 10^{6}\}</annotation></semantics></math>
with the other simulation settings fixed;
<span id="A2.SS7.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(ii) Poisson’s ratio variation</span>, where <math id="A2.SS7.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ν</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu</annotation></semantics></math> is varied over
<math id="A2.SS7.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{0.2,0.25,0.3,0.35,0.4\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.25</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.35</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{0.2,0.25,0.3,0.35,0.4\}</annotation></semantics></math>
with the other simulation settings fixed; and
<span id="A2.SS7.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(iii) material-model variation</span>, where we evaluated seven material settings: two Newtonian fluids, two non-Newtonian fluids, two plasticine materials, and one sand model, with parameters following the PAC-NeRF dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS7.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS7.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Geometry axis.</span>
For each material variation, we evaluated reconstruction performance under the following three geometry settings:
<span id="A2.SS7.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(a) external-shape variation</span>, where the five external shapes from the SfC dataset are used while the cavity is fixed at the center with size <math id="A2.SS7.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>;
<span id="A2.SS7.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(b) cavity-size variation</span>, where the external shape is fixed to a sphere and the cavity size follows the size-variation setting of the main SfC benchmark; and
<span id="A2.SS7.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(c) cavity-position variation</span>, where the external shape is fixed to a sphere and the cavity position follows the position-variation setting of the main SfC benchmark.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS7.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.7.1 </span>Robustness to Young’s Modulus</h4>

<div id="A2.SS7.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS7.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ B.7 Robustness to Material Variations ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> summarizes reconstruction results under Young’s modulus variations across the three geometry settings.
Our method maintains stable performance across stiffness values and consistently improves over SfC-NeRF, indicating robustness to changes in material stiffness.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS7.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.7.2 </span>Robustness to Poisson’s Ratio</h4>

<div id="A2.SS7.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS7.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T18" title="Table 18 ‣ B.7 Robustness to Material Variations ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a> summarizes reconstruction results under Poisson’s ratio variations across the three geometry settings.
Our method maintains stable performance across the evaluated values and consistently improves over SfC-NeRF, indicating robustness to changes in Poisson’s ratio.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS7.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.7.3 </span>Robustness to Material Models</h4>

<div id="A2.SS7.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS7.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T19" title="Table 19 ‣ B.7 Robustness to Material Variations ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a> summarizes reconstruction results under different material models across the three geometry settings.
Our method consistently improves over SfC-NeRF across material categories and geometric variations, indicating that the framework remains effective beyond the elastic setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS7.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS7.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS7.SSS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Summary.</span>
Our method consistently improves over SfC-NeRF across a wide range of elastic parameters and material models.
These results indicate that the proposed hypothesis-space reasoning framework remains robust to material variations beyond the default elastic setting.</p>
</div>

<tr id="A2.T20.3.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A2.T20.3.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.5pt;padding-right:4.5pt;"><span id="A2.T20.3.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">SfC-NeRF (default)</span></th>

<td id="A2.T20.3.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.5pt;padding-right:4.5pt;"><span id="A2.T20.3.3.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1,000</span></td>
<td id="A2.T20.3.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.5pt;padding-right:4.5pt;"><span id="A2.T20.3.3.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1,000</span></td>
<td id="A2.T20.3.3.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.5pt;padding-right:4.5pt;"><span id="A2.T20.3.3.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">0.165</span></td>
<td id="A2.T20.3.3.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.5pt;padding-right:4.5pt;"><span id="A2.T20.3.3.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">0.135</span></td>
<td id="A2.T20.3.3.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.5pt;padding-right:4.5pt;"><span id="A2.T20.3.3.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">0.281</span></td>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 20: </span>Computational budget and reconstruction accuracy on the SfC benchmark.
<em id="A2.T20.13" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Global fwd. evals</em> denotes the number of forward-only MPM simulations used by the global stage.
<em id="A2.T20.14" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Local grad. iters</em> denotes the number of gradient-based differentiable-simulation iterations.
For SfC-NeRF, this corresponds to density-optimization iterations; for ours, to Lagrangian particle refinement iterations.
<em id="A2.T20.15" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Total budget</em> is reported as the sum of these counts for comparison, although forward-only global evaluations are cheaper than forward–backward gradient iterations and use fewer frames.
CD values are scaled by <math id="A2.T20.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{3}</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.8 </span>Runtime Analysis</h3>

<div id="A2.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide additional details for the complexity discussion in Section <a href="#S4.SS5" title="4.5 Implementation and Complexity ‣ 4 Method: Hypothesis-Space Reasoning ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.5</span></a> of the main paper.
The proposed framework has two computationally different components: global hypothesis optimization uses forward-only MPM simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, whereas Lagrangian particle refinement uses forward–backward differentiable MPM simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>.
A single global evaluation requires less computation than a single local refinement iteration because it involves no backward pass and uses only collision-adjacent frames, whereas each local refinement iteration backpropagates through the full observed sequence.
We therefore report the numbers of forward-only global evaluations and gradient-based optimization iterations separately.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">SfC-NeRF optimizes densities through differentiable simulation for 1,000 iterations under its default setting.
Our method uses 250 forward-only simulations for coarse-to-fine global hypothesis optimization, followed by 2,000 iterations of Lagrangian particle refinement.
To assess whether the improvement can be explained simply by a larger optimization budget, we also evaluated an extended SfC-NeRF baseline with 2,300 optimization iterations, giving a comparable count-based budget to our method.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T20" title="Table 20 ‣ B.7.3 Robustness to Material Models ‣ B.7 Robustness to Material Variations ‣ Appendix B Additional Experiments and Analysis ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a> shows that increasing the number of SfC-NeRF iterations does not improve reconstruction accuracy.
In contrast, our method achieves substantially lower CD and higher F-score with a comparable budget.
This indicates that the improvement comes from changing the optimization structure—evaluating explicit structural hypotheses before local refinement—rather than from increasing the number of gradient-based iterations.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS8.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS8.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We also measured representative wall-clock runtime on a sphere sequence with cavity size <math id="A2.SS8.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mn>3</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> using a single H100 GPU.
A forward-only global evaluation on collision-adjacent frames takes about 12 s, whereas one forward–backward local refinement iteration over the full observed sequence takes about 48 s on this sequence.
As a result, the 250-evaluation global search accounts for roughly 3% of the local-refinement runtime.
This supports the practical feasibility of using a moderate global search budget before local refinement.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Qualitative Results</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide additional qualitative comparisons that complement Fig. <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Main Results on the SfC Benchmark ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> of the main paper.
These examples show how the proposed framework behaves under cavity position and size variations, as well as interior-topology stress tests.
Supplementary videos for Fig. <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Main Results on the SfC Benchmark ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and the examples below are available on the <a href="https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/sfc-hypothesis/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">project page</a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>SfC Benchmark</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first present qualitative reconstruction results on the SfC benchmark, which contains controlled variations in cavity position and size.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.1.1 </span>Cavity Position Variations</h4>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ C.1.1 Cavity Position Variations ‣ C.1 SfC Benchmark ‣ Appendix C Qualitative Results ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> shows representative results for two objects under cavity position variation.
SfC-NeRF often reconstructs fragmented or irregular cavity structures, which can lead to post-collision dynamics that deviate from the observation.
In contrast, our method reconstructs more coherent internal structures that better match the ground truth.
The stage-wise results further show how each component contributes: cavity instantiation provides an initial structure, global hypothesis optimization improves the coarse cavity configuration, and Lagrangian particle refinement adjusts local geometry.
These differences become more apparent in post-collision frames, where inaccurate cavity configurations lead to different deformation patterns.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">C.1.2 </span>Cavity Size Variations</h4>

<div id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A3.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ C.1.2 Cavity Size Variations ‣ C.1 SfC Benchmark ‣ Appendix C Qualitative Results ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> shows representative results for two objects under cavity size variation.
In this setting, cavity instantiation already captures the coarse cavity extent, leading to smaller differences across stages than in the position-variation setting.
Nevertheless, Lagrangian particle refinement improves local geometric consistency and leads to more stable post-collision dynamics.
These results suggest that, under cavity-size variation, refinement mainly improves physical consistency and local geometry rather than resolving a large positional ambiguity.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F8" class="ltx_figure">

<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Interior-Topology Stress Tests</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figures <a href="#A3.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ C.2 Interior-Topology Stress Tests ‣ Appendix C Qualitative Results ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>–<a href="#A3.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ C.2 Interior-Topology Stress Tests ‣ Appendix C Qualitative Results ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> show representative qualitative results for the interior-topology stress tests, covering symmetric (<span id="A3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">snowman</span>), asymmetric (<span id="A3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">pacman</span>), and complex (<span id="A3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">split sphere</span>) cavities.
Following Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.4 Interior-Topology Stress Tests ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> of the main paper, we visualized the known-size setting and two stronger structural-assumption settings.
Under the known-size setting, our method produces more coherent cavity structures than SfC-NeRF, although exact reconstruction remains challenging for complex cavities.
With a set of candidate templates and a known center, the global stage can select among structural alternatives before refinement.
Because the candidate set includes the ground-truth template, this setting can produce results close to the known-template setting, suggesting that hypothesis-level selection can identify a plausible structural alternative from the candidate set.
With a known template and center, the remaining ambiguity is mainly orientation, further constraining the reconstruction problem.
These results are consistent with the quantitative trends in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.4 Interior-Topology Stress Tests ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> of the main paper: hypothesis-space reasoning improves reconstruction in the interior-topology stress tests, while exact recovery of complex interior topology remains difficult from collision observations alone.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Summary.</span>
These qualitative examples support the quantitative findings: global hypothesis optimization improves coarse cavity selection, and Lagrangian particle refinement improves local geometry and post-collision consistency.
They also clarify the scope of the framework: stronger structural assumptions can improve reconstruction in the interior-topology stress tests, but complex cavities remain challenging when the observations do not provide sufficient evidence.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<figure id="A3.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.07900v1/qualitative_symmetric.png" id="A3.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/271;" width="685" height="271" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A3.F9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="A3.F9.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Qualitative results for the symmetric subset of the interior-topology stress tests.
We show a representative <span id="A3.F9.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">snowman</span> cavity.
Columns correspond to (a) observation, (b) ground truth, (c) SfC-NeRF under the known-size setting, (d) our method under the known-size setting, (e) our method with a set of candidate templates and a known center, and (f) our method with a known template and center.
Rows correspond to the initial frame (<math id="A3.F9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>), the collision moment, and a post-collision frame.
The visualization follows the hypothesis-space settings in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.4 Interior-Topology Stress Tests ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> of the main paper.
Stronger structural assumptions constrain the hypothesis space and improve reconstruction consistency.
Corresponding supplementary videos are available on the <a href="https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/sfc-hypothesis/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">project page</a>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A3.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.07900v1/qualitative_asymmetric.png" id="A3.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/271;" width="685" height="271" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A3.F10.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 10</span>: </span><span id="A3.F10.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Qualitative results for the asymmetric subset of the interior-topology stress tests.
We show a representative <span id="A3.F10.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">pacman</span> cavity.
Columns correspond to (a) observation, (b) ground truth, (c) SfC-NeRF under the known-size setting, (d) our method under the known-size setting, (e) our method with a set of candidate templates and a known center, and (f) our method with a known template and center.
Rows correspond to the initial frame (<math id="A3.F10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>), the collision moment, and a post-collision frame.
The visualization follows the hypothesis-space settings in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.4 Interior-Topology Stress Tests ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> of the main paper.
The asymmetric cavity introduces a preferred orientation, making this example useful for visualizing how candidate templates and orientation refinement affect reconstruction.
Corresponding supplementary videos are available on the <a href="https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/sfc-hypothesis/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">project page</a>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A3.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2611.07900v1/qualitative_complex.png" id="A3.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:685/271;" width="685" height="271" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A3.F11.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 11</span>: </span><span id="A3.F11.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Qualitative results for the complex subset of the interior-topology stress tests.
We show a representative <span id="A3.F11.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">split sphere</span> cavity.
Columns correspond to (a) observation, (b) ground truth, (c) SfC-NeRF under the known-size setting, (d) our method under the known-size setting, (e) our method with a set of candidate templates and a known center, and (f) our method with a known template and center.
Rows correspond to the initial frame (<math id="A3.F11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>), the collision moment, and a post-collision frame.
The visualization follows the hypothesis-space settings in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.4 Interior-Topology Stress Tests ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> of the main paper.
Exact reconstruction remains challenging for complex cavities from collision observations alone, but hypothesis-space reasoning produces more coherent structures and more physically plausible deformation dynamics.
Corresponding supplementary videos are available on the <a href="https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/sfc-hypothesis/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">project page</a>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
